extracted.intended_audience: literary correspondents / contributors to 19th-century 'Annuals' and editors (friends and literary acquaintances of Charles Lamb)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for contributing short poetic pieces and for editing/reprinting classic works aimed at the nineteenth‑century literary annual market; includes preferred length, stylistic reservations about 'Annuals', and recommendations on handling illustrations and modernization. Framed as private correspondence but contains actionable editorial/submission preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse length limit
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asked for a contribution (an 'incognita') Lamb specifies a strict maximum length: ten lines. He also proposes a topical focus for this particular brief: 'Ten lines about the blue sky of her country will do.' Use very short, tightly focussed pieces for Annual contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contributing to 'Annuals' (preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: I detest to appear in an Annual. ... I hate the paper, the type, the gloss, the dandy plates, the names of contributors poked up into your eyes in first page, and whisked through all the covers of magazines, the barefaced sort of emulation, the immodest candidateship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb advises against appearing in the fashionable 'Annuals' — he finds them gaudy and commercially-minded, with showy production values (glossy paper, dandy plates) and ostentatious self-promotion of contributors. His practical implication: avoid association with these annuals if you value modesty, sincerity, or literary taste; if compelled to appear, expect to be 'cheated' by booksellers and to receive little editorial respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original illustrative style in reprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be done for B. but to reprint the old cuts in as homely but good a style as possible,—the Vanity Fair and the Pilgrims there; the silly-soothness in his setting-out countenance; the Christian idiocy (in a good sense) of his admiration ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing a new edition of a classic (example: Bunyan's Pilgrim), prefer retaining the original, homely illustrations and straightforward style rather than commissioning fashionable or elaborate new designs and plates. Avoid enamelled/overworked designs and sentimental poetic accompaniments that change the character of the original work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid modernizing or 'refitting' archaic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: His cockle-hat and staff transformed to a smart cocked beaver and a jemmy cane; his amice gray to the last Regent Street cut; and his painful palmer's pace to the modern swagger! Stop thy friend's sacrilegious hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not update or modernize the costume, manners, or tone of older, archetypal figures (here, Bunyan's pilgrim) into contemporary fashion: such changes vulgarize and distort the original's character. Maintain the historical/symbolic integrity of original imagery and mannerisms in editorial treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substance over show in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Show me any such poetry in any one of the fifteen forthcoming combinations of show and emptiness 'yclept "Annuals."' ... So there's verses for thy verses; and now let me tell you that the sight of your hand gladdened me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb criticizes the Annuals for providing 'show and emptiness' — the merit criterion here is the poem's substantive content and sincerity rather than decorative display. For contributors: aim for genuine feeling, compact expression, and avoid producing verses that exist only as ornament for a lavish publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtly/professional pronunciation standard (anecdotally)
rubrics_metrics.description: He said that might be in common parlance, or that we might so use it speaking of the 'Heir-at-Law,' a comedy; but that in the law-courts it was necessary to give it a full aspiration, and to say Hayer; he thought it might even vitiate a cause if a counsel pronounced it otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal guidance about professional register: in formal/legal contexts, adopt the more aspirated/pronounced form ('Hayer' for 'heir') to meet courtly/professional expectations. (This appears as a conversational remark but functions as a prescriptive norm for orators/counsel.)
